pdt7y6-e90341.summary: Peter's division of Lombard's text for distinction 37, which turns from things' existence in God to God's existence in things. The first part sets out the true modes of presence: in general (by nature and by grace, confirmed by authorities), by grace in the saints (where God dwelt before them, the indwelling of the whole Trinity, its extension to infants), and by nature in all things, which is incomprehensible and should not be presumptuously explained. The second part removes false modes: God undergoes no local or temporal change, a related doubt about the local motion of spirits is resolved, and Lombard reaffirms that God is everywhere though not locally. The division sets the agenda for the questions that follow on God's presence in things, his relation to place and motion, and the location and motion of angels.
claims: Distinction 37 treats God's presence in things, by nature and by grace.
God is everywhere without local presence or change.
The motion of created spirits is treated as an incidental question.

pdt7y6-e90341-d1e103.summary: Rubric of distinction 37, giving the title of Lombard's chapter: in what ways God is said to be in things.

pdt7y6-e90341-d1e730.summary: Opening division of Lombard's text for distinction 37. Having treated how things exist in God (in the preceding distinctions), Lombard now treats how God exists in things: first he sets out the true modes in which God is in things, then ('Cumque natura divina') removes the false modes in which he is not.
claims: Distinction 37 turns from the existence of things in God to the existence of God in things.
The distinction first gives the true modes of divine presence and then excludes the false ones.

pdt7y6-e90341-d1e752.summary: Subdivides the first part. Lombard treats (1) the mode of God's existence in things in general, by nature or by grace, assigning the modes and confirming them by authorities ('Ne autem ista'); (2) specifically existence by grace ('In sanctis vero'): how God dwells in the saints, where he dwelt before there were saints, that the whole Trinity indwells, and that he dwells not only in adults but also in infants; and (3) specifically existence by nature ('Ex praedictis patet'): that the way God is in all things by nature is incomprehensible, a rebuke of some who presume to explain it, and a related doubt raised and resolved.
claims: Lombard treats God's presence in general, then by grace, then by nature.
The whole Trinity dwells in the saints, including baptized infants.
God's mode of presence by nature in all things is incomprehensible.

pdt7y6-e90341-d1e804.summary: Subdivides the second part, which removes false modes of divine presence. Lombard (1) removes both local and temporal change from God and confirms this with Augustine; (2) raises and settles a related doubt about the local motion of spirits, excluding a false opinion and concluding the truth ('Sunt ergo'); and (3) repeats and confirms that God is everywhere though not locally ('Fateamur'), explaining why he treated the matter ('Iam sufficienter').
claims: God undergoes neither local nor temporal change.
God is everywhere but not locally.
The question of how created spirits move locally arises incidentally from the treatment of divine presence.
